questions.q: What is the correct IUPAC name for CH₃–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–CH₂–OH?
questions.a: Correct answer: **Hexan-2-ol** (or 2-Hexanol). The longest chain containing the –OH group has 6 carbons (hexane), the –OH gets the lowest possible locant (C-2), and the methyl substituent is at C-4 (numbering from the end nearer to –OH). A wrong answer like "4-methylpentan-1-ol" reveals the student selected a 5-carbon chain instead of the 6-carbon chain, violating the "longest chain containing the functional group" rule.

questions.q: Why is the compound CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–CO–CH₃ named Pentan-2-one and not Pentan-3-one?
questions.a: Correct answer: Numbering starts from the end that gives the carbonyl carbon the **lowest locant** (2 vs 3). The functional group (ketone) has priority over alkyl substituents, so the chain is numbered to minimize the locant of the C=O group. A wrong answer claiming "both are correct" or choosing 3-one reveals the student thinks numbering minimizes substituent locants rather than the principal functional group locant.

questions.q: Write the condensed structural formula for 3-bromo-4-methylhex-2-enoic acid.
questions.a: Correct answer: **CH₃–CH=C(Br)–CH(CH₃)–CH₂–COOH** (or CH₃CH=C(Br)CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH). Steps: (1) Parent = hex-2-enoic acid → 6-carbon chain with –COOH at C-1 and C=C at C-2. (2) Numbering: COOH carbon is C-1. (3) Substituents: Br at C-3, CH₃ at C-4. (4) Double bond geometry not specified (E/Z). A wrong formula placing Br at C-4 or the double bond at C-3 reveals confusion about numbering direction relative to the principal functional group (–COOH).

questions.q: Compare the naming of CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–NH₂ and CH₃–CH₂–CH₂–OH. Why does the amine use the suffix "-amine" while the alcohol uses "-ol", and how does numbering differ?
questions.a: Correct answer: Both are named by replacing the terminal '-e' of the parent alkane (propane) with the suffix: **-amine** for –NH₂ (propan-1-amine) and **-ol** for –OH (propan-1-ol). Numbering gives the functional group the lowest locant (C-1 in both cases). The priority order (alcohol > amine) only matters when **both groups are present in the same molecule** — then –OH gets the suffix and –NH₂ becomes the prefix "amino". A student who thinks amine always gets lower priority than alcohol in all contexts misunderstands that priority applies only to **polyfunctional compounds**.

questions.q:
A student names the compound below as "3-ethyl-2-methylpentane". Identify the error and give the correct IUPAC name.
```
    CH₃
     |
CH₃–CH–CH–CH₂–CH₃
     |
    CH₂–CH₃
```
questions.a: Correct answer: The longest chain has **7 carbons** (heptane), not 5. The correct name is **4-methylheptane** (or 4-methylheptane). The student incorrectly chose a 5-carbon chain with two substituents instead of the 7-carbon straight chain. This reveals the classic error of selecting the "most substituted" or "branched-looking" chain rather than the **longest continuous carbon chain**.

questions.q: Design a C₆H₁₂O₂ isomer that contains both an ester and a chloro substituent. Write its IUPAC name and bond-line structure.
questions.a: Example answer: **Ethyl 3-chloropropanoate** (or Ethyl 3-chloropropanoate). Structure: Cl–CH₂–CH₂–COO–CH₂–CH₃. Bond-line: three-carbon chain with C=O at C-1, O–CH₂CH₃ attached to carbonyl, Cl on C-3. Criteria for a good answer: (1) Molecular formula C₆H₁₁ClO₂ (C₆H₁₂O₂ + Cl replaces H), (2) ester suffix "-oate", (3) alkoxy part named as alkyl (ethyl), (4) chloro prefix with correct locant on acid chain. A poor answer might name it as a carboxylic acid with ethoxy substituent, showing confusion about ester nomenclature priority.
